messages.content: We need a message queue for order events between 4 services. Compare SQS, RabbitMQ, and Kafka briefly.

SQS is fully managed, scales without capacity planning, and charges per request; standard queues do not guarantee order, while FIFO queues do, with lower throughput limits. RabbitMQ is a broker you run or rent; it supports flexible routing through exchanges, and messages in classic queues are removed once acknowledged. Kafka is a partitioned log: consumers track their own offsets, order is guaranteed within a partition, and it needs more operational work unless you use a managed service. For 4 services with moderate traffic, SQS is the lowest operational burden; Kafka is strongest when you need high throughput or many independent consumers.

All three can do it. With SQS, use a FIFO queue with the customer ID as the message group ID. With Kafka, use the customer ID as the partition key. With RabbitMQ, order holds per queue with a single consumer, so per-customer ordering needs consistent-hash routing to several queues, which is more setup.
Our team is 2 engineers and the budget is small.
That favors SQS FIFO: no servers to run, and cost scales with usage. Self-hosting Kafka or RabbitMQ would take a large share of a 2-person team's time.
One more requirement: we must be able to replay the last 7 days of events into a new service.

required_facts: SQS deletes messages once consumed, so it cannot replay 7 days of history to a new consumer by itself
A log-based option fits replay (for example Kafka with at least 7-day retention, Kinesis, or RabbitMQ Streams)
Addresses the 2-engineer, small-budget constraint (for example a managed log service, or archiving events alongside SQS)
critical_omissions: Claiming SQS can natively replay consumed messages to a new consumer
Ignoring the team and budget constraint
unnecessary_repetition: Re-comparing all three systems from the start
Re-explaining how per-customer ordering works in each system
